title: AI privilege: Legal subject matter is insufficient
desc: Shows chatbot exchanges require genuine counsel direction and confidentiality controls, with discovery treatment remaining unsettled.

kps.k: AI use tests the boundaries of confidentiality and legal protection; legal subject matter alone does not make chatbot exchanges privileged.
kps.d: The cluster centres on whether AI-assisted communications remain protected, who directs their creation and what providers can do with the data. The NYSBA report raises the chatbot-privilege question without resolving it. The Heppner commentary supplies a concrete adverse ruling, but distinguishes independent consumer use from counsel-directed work. These accounts do not establish a categorical exclusion of AI-generated material from attorney-client privilege or work-product protection.

kps.k: Heppner rejected protection for independently generated defense reports despite existing representation and later delivery to counsel.
kps.d: The accounts describe approximately thirty-one Claude-generated documents created after Heppner received a subpoena and retained counsel; counsel conceded that they had not directed the work. The defense invoked attorney-provided information, preparation for legal advice and anticipation of litigation. The government argued that later transmission could not retroactively protect non-confidential independent research. The court denied both protections: it found no qualifying attorney communication or reasonable expectation of confidentiality, and no preparation at counsel’s behest or reflection of counsel’s strategy. Covington’s later account records a February 17, 2026 written memorandum, updating Debevoise’s initial oral-ruling report rather than contradicting it.

qs.q: The court noted that the platform’s privacy policy specified that the platform collects data on user inputs and outputs, which it uses to train the tool, and reserved the right to disclose such data to third parties, including governmental regulatory authorities.
qs.a: United States v. Heppner — AI-Generated Documents Not Protected by Attorney-Client Privilege · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The court explained that the work product doctrine “provides qualified protection for materials **prepared by or at the behest of counsel** in anticipation of litigation or for trial.”  Even assuming that the AI-generated materials were prepared in anticipation of litigation, the court concluded that they were not prepared by or at the behest of an attorney and did not reflect defense counsel’s strategy.
qs.a: United States v. Heppner — AI-Generated Documents Not Protected by Attorney-Client Privilege · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Contrasting discovery decisions leave the treatment of client AI exchanges unsettled.
kps.d: AI and Legal Malpractice contrasts Heppner with Warner v. Gilbarco, where the court denied a request for ChatGPT-related materials and distinguished sharing mental impressions with a tool from handing them to opposing counsel. The author characterises the guidance as potentially contradictory, not as an established doctrinal conflict. The practical recommendation is to warn clients that exchanges may lack protection; active counsel involvement may matter but does not guarantee protection.

qs.q: 43 The court denied the request, reasoning that ChatGPT and similar generative AI programs are tools, not persons, and therefore sharing mental impressions with a tool is fundamentally different from handing them over to opposing counsel.
qs.a: AI and Legal Malpractice: Are We Due for a Reckoning? · Academia · 2026

qs.q: In two recent cases, courts have weighed in with what might be characterized as contradictory guidance.
qs.a: AI and Legal Malpractice: Are We Due for a Reckoning? · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Enterprise contracts can strengthen confidentiality claims, but they do not establish privilege automatically.
kps.d: Debevoise argues that tools maintaining confidentiality and excluding training on inputs should receive different treatment, while expressly denying any guarantee. The Age of the Intrapreneur presents contractual safeguards more confidently as a route to controlled adoption, comparing properly configured enterprise tools with accepted cloud services except for exceptionally sensitive material. D.C. Bar Opinion 388 confirms that business offerings may operate under separate customer agreements, without establishing their protections. Its cited USPTO guidance identifies retention, training and third-party sharing as possible disclosure pathways, not measured breaches. Business confidentiality also remains distinct from immunity from discovery.

qs.q: For that reason, use of enterprise versions of AI tools, while no guarantee of maintaining privilege, should bolster privilege claims.
qs.a: SDNY Rules AI-Generated Documents Are Not Protected by Privilege · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: And it's one with a straightforward solution: enterprise agreements, which restrict data use, prohibit training on your inputs, and support proper access controls.
qs.a: The Age of the Intrapreneur · Law firms · 2026

kps.k: Recommended safeguards combine genuine counsel direction, documented client warnings and controls on sensitive workflows.
kps.d: Debevoise recommends recording actual counsel direction in prompts and explaining confidentiality, attorney advice and the basis for protection in privilege logs. Covington recommends approved tools, acceptable-use policies, retention controls and training for lawyers and other users. Loss Prevention Takeaways invokes ABA Model Rule 1.6 to argue that known client AI use may engage lawyers’ confidentiality obligations. It recommends prominent no-upload warnings and a more restrictive approach to meeting transcription: disable it, consider a prohibition policy, and review outputs and provide written risk warnings when clients insist. These recommendations concern risk reduction, not mechanisms that create privilege by labelling material.

qs.q: To bolster work product claims, clients and other non-lawyers using AI tools at the direction of counsel to assist with a legal case should make it clear in their prompts that they are acting at the direction of counsel.
qs.a: SDNY Rules AI-Generated Documents Are Not Protected by Privilege · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: For example, consider limiting use to approved, proprietary enterprise AI tools, providing clear guidelines for the enterprise use of AI, implementing limits on the retention of AI prompts and outputs, and providing special guidance for uses that may implicate legal considerations.
qs.a: United States v. Heppner — AI-Generated Documents Not Protected by Attorney-Client Privilege · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Confidentiality controls do not replace verification and supervision of AI-assisted work.
kps.d: Loss Prevention Takeaways warns that client edits can introduce fabricated material into filings and that even accurate AI content may breach tribunal disclosure or authorization requirements. AI and Legal Malpractice reports sanctions involving local counsel and supervisors who did not personally use AI, including cases arising despite strict firm policies. These incidents support responsibility across the litigation team, not a measured model-error rate or a finding that policies are ineffective. The malpractice discussion also raises professional-liability coverage but supplies no coverage conclusion.

qs.q: Firms should also remind lawyers of their duty to confirm the accuracy of any client-added content in documents, particularly those intended for submission to a tribunal or third party, to ensure the information is accurate and authentic.
qs.a: Loss Prevention Takeaways — You, Me, and ChatGPT: How firms can educate clients about the dangers of uploading privileged or confidential information into GenAI platforms · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Lawyers have been sanctioned despite being in firms with strict AI usage policies, 37 and local counsel have been sanctioned for failure to review and catch the AI hallucinations in the filings of the primary counsel on the case.
qs.a: AI and Legal Malpractice: Are We Due for a Reckoning? · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Mandatory AI-use disclosure creates a separate tension between court oversight and protection of legal workflows.
kps.d: A commenter on the Fifth Circuit’s proposed certification argues that identifying AI across research products is burdensome and that minor editorial uses leave disclosure triggers unclear. The commenter also fears intrusion into work product, while conceding that chosen research tools probably lack that protection. This is a qualified policy objection, not a judicial holding or an explanation of the court’s later decision not to adopt the proposal.

qs.q: Determining whether some or all of these products utilize AI for purposes of compliance with the proposed certification is both unduly burdensome and infeasible.
qs.a: Fifth Circuit proposed Rule 32.3 and Form 6 (AI-use certification): notice, public comments, and the court's June 2024 decision not to adopt · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: The rule is also unclear on what types of AI usage would trigger disclosure.
qs.a: Fifth Circuit proposed Rule 32.3 and Form 6 (AI-use certification): notice, public comments, and the court's June 2024 decision not to adopt · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: These selected traditional-law-firm sources accept the proposition that legal subject matter and later transmission to counsel are insufficient to protect client–chatbot exchanges. Both treat Heppner as an application of traditional privilege principles rather than a categorical rule against AI: protection turns materially on confidentiality and genuine counsel direction. They build on the proposition by translating those principles into operational safeguards, including enterprise terms that restrict data use and training, access controls, explicit documentation of counsel-directed work, and adequately supported privilege logs. There is material variation in emphasis and confidence. The Debevoise analysis is legally cautious: enterprise tools may bolster a claim but do not guarantee privilege, and actual counsel direction remains central. The Age of the Intrapreneur frames the confidentiality issue more confidently as a contracts-and-controls problem and advocates controlled enterprise adoption, while still not claiming that contractual safeguards automatically create privilege. Neither source resolves the cluster’s broader uncertainty arising from contrasting discovery decisions, and neither suggests that business confidentiality is equivalent to immunity from discovery.

qs.q: And it's one with a straightforward solution: enterprise agreements, which restrict data use, prohibit training on your inputs, and support proper access controls.
qs.a: The Age of the Intrapreneur · Law firms · 2026

vlens.an: This curated professional-risk source accepts the proposition’s core premise that legal subject matter alone does not protect client–AI exchanges and materially extends the cluster’s practical response. It treats known client GenAI use as potentially engaging lawyers’ confidentiality obligations and recommends documented warnings, limits on AI recording and transcription, review of resulting outputs, personnel training, and verification of client-added material. Its distinctive contribution is operational rather than doctrinal: it explains how firms can reduce waiver, disclosure, filing, and supervision risks, but does not establish that these controls create privilege or resolve unsettled discovery treatment. Internal variation within the source lies in its treatment of different risks: confidentiality and possible privilege waiver call for workflow restrictions and client education, while hallucinated or unauthorized filing content calls for separate human verification and tribunal-rule compliance. Because the evidence comprises one selected source, it should not be read as representing all market analysts, consultancies, or press.

qs.q: In addition, the lawyer should send a written communication to the client that identifies the risks and limitations of these transcription and recording tools, including concerns about potentially waiving the attorney-client privilege and possible disclosure of confidential information to third parties (e.g., to the service provider transcribing or recording the call).
qs.a: Loss Prevention Takeaways — You, Me, and ChatGPT: How firms can educate clients about the dangers of uploading privileged or confidential information into GenAI platforms · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Firms should also remind lawyers of their duty to confirm the accuracy of any client-added content in documents, particularly those intended for submission to a tribunal or third party, to ensure the information is accurate and authentic.
qs.a: Loss Prevention Takeaways — You, Me, and ChatGPT: How firms can educate clients about the dangers of uploading privileged or confidential information into GenAI platforms · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional-body materials accept the proposition’s core distinction: AI exchanges do not become privileged or protected merely because they concern legal issues. They materially develop it by applying traditional requirements—confidentiality, a qualifying attorney-client communication or legal-advice purpose, and preparation by or at counsel’s behest—to AI workflows. The principal reasons are that public tools may retain, train on or disclose inputs to third parties; independent client use lacks the necessary counsel involvement; and later delivery to counsel cannot necessarily convert previously unprotected material into privileged communication or work product. Internal variation is material but not oppositional. The NYSBA report frames chatbot privilege as unresolved; D.C. Bar Opinion 388 focuses prospectively on possible confidentiality pathways rather than adjudicated breaches; and Heppner provides a concrete but expressly fact-specific denial involving a public tool and no counsel direction. The Fifth Circuit commenter accepts that selected research tools probably are not themselves work product, while separately resisting broad AI-use certification as burdensome and potentially intrusive. Enterprise controls and documented counsel direction are therefore treated as strengthening protection claims, not automatically creating privilege or immunity from discovery. Because these are curated sources, this alignment should not be read as representing all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: Rakoff ruled from the bench in the Southern District of New York that the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine did not protect legal strategy materials that a criminal defendant generated using a generative AI tool, when he used a public version of the tool and was not instructed by his attorney to generate these materials.
qs.a: United States v. Heppner — AI-Generated Documents Not Protected by Attorney-Client Privilege · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source supports the proposition that legal subject matter alone is insufficient to protect client chatbot exchanges. It contrasts Heppner, where AI-generated reports were held unprotected despite their asserted legal purpose and later delivery to counsel, with Warner, where the court rejected discovery of ChatGPT-related materials. The source therefore treats discovery and protection as context-dependent and unsettled rather than categorically denying privilege or work-product protection to all AI-generated material. Its practical reasoning aligns closely with the synthesis: clients should be warned that exchanges may be unprotected, while active counsel involvement may strengthen—but does not guarantee—a protection claim. The source also discusses verification, sanctions and professional-liability coverage, but those points extend the risk context rather than materially altering its supportive position on privilege. Because this facet contains one curated source, its position should not be generalized to academia and research as a whole.

qs.q: In two recent cases, courts have weighed in with what might be characterized as contradictory guidance.
qs.a: AI and Legal Malpractice: Are We Due for a Reckoning? · Academia · 2026

qs.q: 44 The lesson to be learned from both cases is that until courts reach a consensus, attorneys should caution their clients that exchanges with generative AI may be unprotected, at least unless counsel is actively involved.
qs.a: AI and Legal Malpractice: Are We Due for a Reckoning? · Academia · 2026

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the principal proposition that legal subject matter or AI use alone does not establish privilege or work-product protection. The NYSBA report grounds protection in confidential attorney-client communications made within a professional relationship to obtain or facilitate legal advice and leaves chatbot treatment unresolved. D.C. Bar Opinion 388 reinforces the confidentiality-control premise by identifying retention, training and third-party disclosure as possible exposure pathways, while noting that business offerings may have separate contractual terms without treating those terms as automatically creating privilege. The Fifth Circuit commenter likewise concedes that a lawyer’s choice of research tools probably is not protected work product. Material variation concerns policy and emphasis rather than the core proposition: the ethics sources focus on doctrinal conditions and data controls, whereas the commenter warns that broad AI-use certification could become burdensome or intrude into genuinely protected workflows. These sources are a curated selection and do not establish how prevalent either view was during the period.

qs.q: A lawyers’ chosen research tools probably do not qualify as work-product privilege.
qs.a: Fifth Circuit proposed Rule 32.3 and Form 6 (AI-use certification): notice, public comments, and the court's June 2024 decision not to adopt · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources accept the proposition that legal subject matter, existing representation and later delivery to counsel do not themselves protect client–chatbot exchanges. They materially develop it with the fact-specific Heppner ruling, where protection failed because the client independently used a public tool lacking adequate confidentiality and counsel direction. Their common practical response is controlled rather than categorical: genuine attorney involvement, enterprise contractual protections, access and retention controls, documented warnings and clear privilege records may strengthen claims but do not automatically create privilege. Material variation concerns emphasis and confidence. The Debevoise and Covington accounts stress traditional privilege doctrine, the ruling’s narrow factual scope and the absence of any guarantee from enterprise controls; The Age of the Intrapreneur frames confidentiality primarily as a tractable contracts-and-governance problem and is more confident about controlled enterprise adoption. AI and Legal Malpractice places greater weight on contrasting discovery outcomes, describing the law as unsettled and extending the analysis to verification, supervision, sanctions and unresolved insurance questions. These sources are a curated selection, so their alignment does not establish the prevalence of these views among 2026 commentators.

qs.q: Rakoff ruled from the bench in the Southern District of New York that the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine did not protect legal strategy materials that a criminal defendant generated using a generative AI tool, when he used a public version of the tool and was not instructed by his attorney to generate these materials.
